{prompt}
prompt: A woman you casually know spots you as you walk through a store , approaches you , smiles and says , `` I saw your gravestone today , just lovely ! '' and nonchalantly strolls away .
content:
I was holding two avocados, squeezing each for ripeness, when Ruth Pellman appeared at my elbow.

I knew Ruth the way you know people in a town of four thousand. She sat two seats down at book club and waved from her Buick. Once she had brought a lemon loaf to a library fundraiser and told me the recipe was "a secret, sweetheart, but I'll die with it, so ask my executor."

She smiled at me, bright and pleasant, with her purse hooked over her forearm.

"I saw your gravestone today," she said. "Just lovely!"

Then she patted my arm, turned her cart toward the cereal aisle, and strolled away humming.

I stood there with an avocado in each hand and felt my face go cold from the forehead down.

Nobody in Harlow Creek knew my name was Dana. Here I was Claire Duvall, a name I'd picked off a paint chip at a hardware store in Tennessee six years ago, in the first week of being nobody. I did bookkeeping from home, grew tomatoes badly, and never posted photographs. I had a lease, a library card, and a life built entirely from things that couldn't be traced.

Dana Whitlock was supposed to be dead in every way that mattered. Nobody had ever told me she had a gravestone.

I put the avocados back, left my cart in the aisle, and walked out past the checkout girl, who said, "Ma'am? Ma'am, you forgot your—" The door cut her off.

---

It took me three hours and a library computer to find it.

Dana Whitlock, beloved wife. The county cemetery in Marion, Ohio, had a volunteer-run website with photographs of headstones, and someone had uploaded a new one two weeks earlier. Gray granite. A rose carved in the corner. My birthday, and under it a death date from the previous spring, which was a lie. I had been sitting in a laundromat in Knoxville that day, folding someone else's towels because I'd lost my own.

Underneath it said: *Gone too soon. Never forgotten. Rest at last in the arms of the one who loved you most.*

I read that last line eleven times.

The one who loved me most was Garrett. Garrett had loved me so much that he'd put the phone in a drawer where I couldn't reach it, so much that he'd driven to my sister's house, then my job, then my sister's job. He had loved me right up to the night I walked out with forty dollars and a coat that didn't fit.

So he had declared me dead. Or he had found a judge willing to, or maybe he had just bought a rock and put my name on it. I didn't know which, and I sat there with my hands flat on the library desk trying to decide which was worse.

Then I started thinking about Ruth.

---

She lived on Alder Street in a yellow house with a ceramic goose on the porch, dressed for the season in a little raincoat. I stood on her walk for a full minute before I knocked.

She opened the door as though she'd been standing behind it. "Claire," she said. "I wondered if it would be today or tomorrow. Come in. I've got coffee on."

"How did you—" My voice cracked, and I tried again. "What did you mean?"

"Sit down, sweetheart. You look like a ghost." She heard herself and gave a dry little laugh. "Well. That's rather the point, isn't it?"

I sat. Her kitchen smelled of cinnamon and radiator heat. She poured two cups and slid one across the table before she spoke.

"My sister's buried in Marion," she said. "Forty years now. I go every March, take her tulips. This year I'm walking back to the car, and there's a new stone three rows over, so shiny it looked wet. I'm nosy, so I went to look. And there's your picture."

"My picture?"

"They put a little oval portrait on it. Porcelain. You're younger and your hair's longer and you look like you're trying to smile for someone who's making you." She stirred her coffee. "But it's your face. I've sat across from it every other Thursday for four years."

My hands had started to shake. I put them in my lap.

"Why would you say it like that?" I asked. "In the grocery store, in the middle of the day, like it was a *compliment*?"

"Because I didn't know who might be listening," Ruth said. "And because I wanted you to hear it the right way, which is the way I meant it." She leaned forward. "Claire, honey, listen. Do you know what it means that he bought you a gravestone?"

"It means he's—"

"It means he *quit*." Her voice was quiet and flat. "A man who's still hunting doesn't bury what he's hunting. He stops the story where he can control it, with a stone and a date and a nice poem about how much he loved you. People will send him casseroles. He gets to be the widower." She tapped the table. "Men like that can't bear a loose end, so he tied you off. He's telling everyone you're finished, and if he ever finds out otherwise, he'd have to explain the stone. He won't want to explain the stone."

I hadn't thought of it that way. I'd been looking at the stone as a threat, but I turned it over in my mind, and Ruth was right that it also worked as a door closing.

"How do you know all this?" I whispered.

Ruth looked toward the window, where the goose stood in its little yellow raincoat.

"I wasn't always Ruth Pellman," she said. "It's a good name. It belonged to a woman who died of pneumonia in 1987 and had no family left. Ask me sometime how you go about acquiring a dead woman's papers. I wouldn't recommend it, but I could tell you." She smiled, and there was something fierce behind it. "I recognized you the first week you came to book club. You sat with your back to the wall, facing the door. You watched who came in. Nobody does that unless they have to."

I started crying then, quietly, the way I'd learned to. Ruth didn't touch me or say anything. She pushed a box of tissues across the table and waited.

"Did you tell anyone?" I managed.

"Heavens, no. Who would I tell? Who would I be to tell?" She sat back. "I only wanted you to know that someone saw it, and that it's a handsome stone. Heavy granite, nice lettering, and he paid good money. That man isn't going to pay for another one, and he isn't going to dig this one up. You're safe in a way you weren't last month."

"It still has my name on it."

"It has *Dana's* name on it," Ruth said gently. "Dana can rest. You never have to be her again."

---

I stayed until the coffee went cold. When I stood to leave, Ruth hugged me with surprising strength, smelling of cinnamon and Jergens lotion.

"Book club's Thursday," she said at the door. "We're doing the one with the lighthouse. Bring the lemon bars you pretend you didn't make from my recipe."

"That was your recipe?"

"Sweetheart, everything good in this town is somebody's secret."

I walked home the long way, under the budding maples. Somewhere in Ohio a slab of gray granite sat in the March light with a rose carved in its corner and my young, unhappy face in porcelain, telling everyone that I was finished. I'd spent six years certain I was a woman running from something, and I was starting to think I might be one who had arrived.

On Thursday I brought the lemon bars. Ruth took one, bit into it, and said, "Just lovely."

Neither of us said anything else about it, and we didn't need to.

prompt: Reddit , as a collective entity , runs for president .
content:
# The Front Page

The filing with the Federal Election Commission was, legally speaking, a disaster.

*Candidate name:* Reddit
*Age:* 19
*Place of birth:* "A dorm room in Virginia, but also the internet, so, uh, everywhere?"
*Natural-born citizen:* "Define natural."

The FEC rejected it in four days. Reddit took the rejection badly, and the thread hit 80,000 comments before the mods locked it. The top comment, with 112,000 upvotes, read:

> **They said we can't run because we're not a person. Fine. We'll find a person.**

That is how Gerald Pruitt, a forty-one-year-old dental-supply salesman from Toledo, became the most scrutinized human being on Earth.

---

I was hired as his campaign manager. In practice I was the Designated Adult, a title that appeared on my contract after a vote of 2.3 million users. I was the only person on the payroll who had ever worked on a campaign. Everyone else was a volunteer, and every volunteer was also a moderator, and every moderator was tired.

"Why me?" Gerald asked on our first day, in a rented office above a vape shop. He was holding a coffee mug that said WORLD'S OKAYEST SALESMAN.

"You posted once in r/mildlyinteresting," I said. "A photo of a potato shaped like Ohio. Four hundred thousand upvotes."

"It was a really good potato."

"They felt it showed character."

He had a small earpiece, a clear plastic curl that fed him the top-voted response to anything anyone asked. The campaign called this the Hivemind Interface. Gerald called it "Steve," because he needed to call it something.

---

The platform took six weeks and nearly tore the country apart.

It was drafted in a thread titled **OFFICIAL PLATFORM MEGATHREAD (READ BEFORE COMMENTING)**. The first draft was good, then it got weird, then it got good again. A user named u/NotARobot_Trust_Me proposed abolishing the penny. It passed instantly. A user named u/SourDoughDave proposed a national right to a nap. It passed with a note: *"Edit: thanks for the gold, kind stranger."*

Healthcare was harder. Eleven thousand people had personal stories, and every one of them was true, and they pointed in different directions. A nurse from Oregon wrote four thousand words that ended: *"I don't care about your ideology, I care that I held a man's hand while he decided whether he could afford the ambulance he was already in."* It reached the top and stayed there. The policy that grew from it was imperfect, but it was real.

Foreign policy collapsed into an argument about whether Australia was a real place.

We also had a Vice Presidential candidate. After a bracket tournament that lasted nine days and ended in a shocking upset, it was a corgi named Biscuit. He was not eligible, and we said so loudly. A seventy-three-year-old retired judge from Tucson named Marguerite Oyelaran, who had been quietly answering legal questions in r/AskLawyers for eleven years, took the actual slot. She accepted by posting:

> **Fine. But the dog stays on the bus.**

---

The campaign had its crises.

The first was The Brigade. Another community, which I won't name, mobilized to vote down every campaign post and flood our rallies with a single repeated joke. For three days Gerald couldn't give a speech without forty thousand people chanting something about a bird.

The second was The Comment. Someone dug up Gerald's account history and found a post from 2012 in which he had, at nineteen, argued with total confidence that a hot dog was a sandwich.

"I stand by it," Gerald told the press, to the horror of everyone. The post gained 600,000 upvotes. His approval rating among people who had never voted before rose eleven points.

The third crisis was the one that almost ended us. We had no message discipline. Reddit contained everyone, so Reddit believed everything. Mondays it wanted to nationalize the railroads. Tuesdays it wanted to abolish the Senate. On Wednesday afternoons, for about ninety minutes, it wanted to be left alone.

"The thing about a hivemind," I told Gerald in a motel parking lot in Iowa, "is that it isn't a mind. It's a mood."

"Steve says you're right," said Gerald, listening. "Steve also says *'This.'*"

---

The first debate was in Cleveland. The opposition was exactly who you'd expect: two seasoned, polished, well-funded candidates who had been preparing for this since birth. They had binders. We had Gerald, a corgi in the green room, and an earpiece that lagged.

For forty minutes it went almost well. A moderator asked about the economy and Steve fed Gerald a clean, upvoted paragraph with a decent joke in it. Gerald delivered it flawlessly, even the pause. The audience laughed. One of the binder candidates looked briefly afraid.

Then the moderator turned to the last question. It had been submitted by a viewer, a woman in Dayton named Colleen, and it was not a policy question.

"My son died of an overdose fourteen months ago," the moderator read. "He was twenty-six. He'd tried to get help three times. I'm not asking what your plan is. I've read all the plans. I'm asking: when you look at a mother like me, what do you actually *see?*"

The room went quiet.

In Gerald's ear, I knew, forty million people were typing at once. I watched the feed on my laptop in the wings. The comments came in a flood: *Be honest. Don't give a speech. Say something real. Say you don't know. Say her son's name. Ask his name.* Then the thread tangled. Top comment, second comment, third comment all swapped places every four seconds. It was a hundred answers and no answer, and the voice in his ear was static.

Gerald stood there for a long moment. Then he reached up, took out the earpiece, and set it on the lectern.

"I don't know what Steve's saying," he said. "I don't think Steve knows either. I'm sorry. I don't think anyone does, right now." He turned to the camera. "Colleen, what was his name?"

A long pause. The feed on my screen had gone completely still.

"Daniel," said the moderator, reading her note. "Daniel Marsh."

"Daniel," Gerald said. "I'd like to say I see a mother whose kid needed a door to be open, and it wasn't, three times. I'd say I see us failing at something we're capable of doing. And I don't have a binder. But I've got about forty million people who'll show up for a stranger at two a.m. if you ask them a hard question, and I think you can do something with that, if you make it a country's job and not just a comment section's."

He paused.

"I'm sorry about Daniel," he said. "That's all I've got."

On my laptop, the thread began to move again. It wasn't a debate. It was just a long column of people typing the same two words, one after another, up and up and up the screen:

> **Daniel Marsh.**
> **Daniel Marsh.**
> **Daniel Marsh.**

---

We lost, of course.

We lost by four points and a rounding error, after a campaign that cost less than one of the binder candidates' catering budgets. Turnout in the 18-to-29 bracket was the highest in the nation's history. Two dozen state legislatures introduced bills based on the platform. One of them, in Ohio, was named after Daniel Marsh, and it passed.

On election night we gathered in the office above the vape shop. Gerald sat on a folding chair with the earpiece in his hand. Marguerite poured the Tucson-brand sparkling cider. Biscuit the corgi, who had been photographed more than any other dog in history, slept under the table.

Gerald would deliver the concession speech from a livestream with a record number of viewers. He hadn't written anything. He just read the top comment from the live thread, which everyone had agreed was the most honest one:

> **Well. That happened.**
>
> **Edit: wow, this blew up. Thanks, kind strangers.**
>
> **Edit 2: no, seriously. Thank you. See you at the next one.**

"I can't say that," Gerald said, laughing.

"You absolutely can," said Marguerite.

He said it. Then, because he was Gerald, he added a sentence of his own, the last words of the campaign, which made the front page of every newspaper in the country the next morning.

"For the record," he said, looking straight into the camera, "a hot dog is a sandwich."

The thread, I'm told, is still open.

prompt: Hawksbill Mountain
content:
# The Bill

On the first cool Saturday of October, Dale Whitaker woke at four in the morning, dressed in the dark, and was sitting on the porch with his boots laced when his daughter came downstairs.

"I'm ready," he said.

Nora stood in the doorway in her socks. The doctors had a word for this, and the pamphlets had a whole section about it. *Sundowning* was for evenings, though, and this was the other end of the day. This was just her father, seventy-one years old, with his thermos between his feet and the look of a man who has been kept waiting.

"Ready for what, Dad?"

He frowned at her kindly, the way he'd frown at a kid who'd forgotten a sandwich. "Hawksbill."

She made coffee. She found her own boots. She did not ask herself whether it was wise, because she had spent eight months asking herself that about everything, and the answer was always *probably not*, and the days were still long.

---

They reached the Hawksbill Gap parking area at sunrise. The ridge was wrapped in a fog that lay along the valleys like milk in a saucer, and the oaks along the Lower Hawksbill Trail had gone copper and rust. Her father got out of the car slowly. For a moment he stood with one hand on the door, looking at nothing, and she saw the fear come over his face. He didn't know where he was.

Then he looked up the slope, where the trail climbed into the trees, and the fear went out of him like breath.

"Well," he said. "There she is."

He started walking.

She had been prepared to lead. She had a printed map, a first-aid kit, and a phone with one bar of service. Instead she found herself following him, because he walked up that trail the way you walk through your own kitchen at night. He stepped over a root before she saw it. He swung wide around a muddy place that wasn't muddy yet, and she realized it would be after the next rain.

"Spring seep," he said over his shoulder. "Comes up right there. Ruins your boots in April."

"You remember that?"

"Of course I remember that," he said, mildly offended, and walked on.

It was the strangest thing. Last Tuesday he had called her by her mother's name and asked when Ruth was getting home from work. Ruth had been dead six years. Nora had said *soon, Dad*, because the pamphlet said not to argue, and had gone into the bathroom and run the water so he wouldn't hear her. But here he named the trees. Here he stopped at a bend and said, "Chestnut stump. Blight got the rest of them before I was born. This one keeps sending up shoots anyway," and sure enough, a thin sapling stood out of the old gray stump, its leaves jagged and yellow.

"They never get big," he said. "Get about twenty feet and the blight finds them. Then the root sends up another one." He touched the stump with two fingers. "Stubborn."

She had to look at the trees for a while after that.

---

The climb was only a mile and a half, but it took them most of two hours. He stopped often, and she let him think it was for the view. Twice he asked her who she was, politely, as if they had met at a trailhead. Both times she said, "I'm Nora. I'm hiking with you today," and both times he said, "Well, good. It's better with company," and went on.

She decided she could live inside that answer. *It's better with company.*

Near the top the trail steepened into rock, the old greenstone that gives the mountain its bones, gray-green and lichen-spotted, laid in steps by men who'd been dead for ninety years. Her father put his palm flat against one of the boulders as he passed it, the way you'd touch a horse.

"CCC boys built this," he said. "My dad's cousin was one. Thirty dollars a month, and twenty-five of it went home." He chuckled. "He said the rocks were all the same size when they started and by the end of summer they were all different sizes, and he swore the rocks were doing it on purpose."

"Did you ever meet him?"

"Who?"

"Your dad's cousin."

He thought about it for a long moment. She watched the thought go out into the fog and not come back.

"I'd like to have," he said finally.

---

The summit was above the cloud. That was what she hadn't expected. The fog had sunk and spread, and the whole Shenandoah Valley lay beneath them as a white sea with the ridges standing out of it like dark islands. The sun was well up, and the light came sideways and gold across the stone platform at the top. A few other hikers had made it up, a couple in matching windbreakers and a young man with a camera. They spoke in the low voices people use in high places.

Her father walked to the edge of the platform and stood with his hands in his jacket pockets.

"You know why they call it Hawksbill?" he said.

"Because of the shape?"

"Because of the shape. From down in the valley, it's got that curve to the ridge. Like a beak." He made the shape in the air with one hand, a hooked line. "Your mother never saw it. Thirty years she said, *Dale, I just don't see it,* and I said, *Ruth, you've got to stand at the right spot.*" He laughed, a real laugh. "I drove her all over Page County trying to find the right spot."

"Did you ever find it?"

"Oh, sure. Little pull-off past Stanley, on 340. Right around sunset." He was quiet. "She looked at it a long time. She said, *Well, I'll be.* That's all. *Well, I'll be.*"

Nora realized she was crying, and that he'd noticed, and that he didn't know why. He turned and looked at her with the worried gentleness that had been her whole childhood.

"Hey, now," he said. "Hey. What's all this?"

"It's just pretty," she said.

"It is," he agreed, and put his arm around her shoulders, and they stood and looked.

Below them, a single bird rose out of the white, a dark shape that tilted on the thermals and climbed without a wingbeat. It crossed the sun and was gone. She would never know whether it was a hawk. She decided it was.

"There," her father said softly. "That's him. That's the one the mountain's named for."

"Dad?"

"Mm."

"Thanks for bringing me."

He considered this, squinting at the horizon. His face was calm, entirely at home.

"Well," he said. "It's better with company."

They stayed until the fog burned off and the valley came up green and gold and ordinary below them. Then they went down together, slowly, his hand on the stones and hers on his elbow. Somewhere on the way he started to hum, a tune she half knew, and she realized it was one her mother used to sing in the kitchen.

At the bend with the chestnut stump, he stopped and touched it again.

"Stubborn," he said, and smiled, and walked on.

content:
# Cubicles & Commutes

The back room of the Drowned Lantern smelled of tallow candles, old ale, and the faint sulfur of a dragon trying not to be noticed.

"Roll for Parking," said Morvane the Lich, peering over his screen of stitched bat leather. His voice rattled like a bag of dry knuckles. "And remember, you're already eleven minutes late."

Grukk the orc, who was a head taller than anyone else at the table and had to sit on a reinforced barrel, picked up the twenty-sided die in two fingers. "Brad does not get nervous," he rumbled.

"Brad's palms are sweating," Morvane said. "Brad has a nine-thirty with Linda from Compliance."

Grukk grimaced and rolled. The die skittered across the table and stopped.

"Natural one," said Pip the goblin, with delight.

"Brad," Morvane intoned, "attempts to parallel park a 2014 Honda Civic. You hit a bollard. You hit the *other* bollard. You are now somehow perpendicular to the curb and a man in a vest is writing you a ticket."

Grukk slammed a fist on the table and the mugs jumped. "I would simply fight the man in the vest."

"Brad would not," said Seraphelle the elf, not looking up from her character sheet. She was the only one who had filled hers out in calligraphy. "Brad has a credit score to think about."

"What is a credit score?"

"It's a number that says how much the village trusts you."

"That is *horrifying*," said Grukk. "Who decides it?"

"Nobody knows," said Morvane, with relish. "That's the beauty of it."

---

They had found the game in the ruins of a human library, or rather, Morvane had. Three hundred years of lichdom left a lot of time for reading, and among the scrolls of forbidden necromancy he had dug up a water-stained box set, *Adulting: The Roleplaying Game*, along with a stack of receipts, a few pamphlets, and a catalogue for something called IKEA, which he treated as sacred scripture.

None of them had ever played anything like it. In every other game they knew, you were a hero. You slew things and plundered things and gave rousing speeches before battle.

In this one you were a *person*. You had a *job*.

"I'll go next," said Seraphelle. "Jessica gets her oat milk latte and—"

"Roll for Small Talk," said Morvane.

She rolled a seventeen. "Jessica says, 'Crazy weather we're having.'"

"A masterwork," Morvane breathed. "The man nods. He says, 'Sure is.' Nothing more is required of either of you. The social contract is upheld."

Seraphelle sat back, glowing. "Eight hundred years I've spent learning to speak to kings. It never occurred to me you could just say a thing about the weather and *leave*."

At the end of the table, Vazrath the Ancient, a dragon of the Ashen Peaks who had shrunk himself to the size of a large cat so he could fit through the tavern door, was reading the rules with one claw very carefully pinning the page.

"I have a question about Dennis," he said.

"Go ahead."

"Dennis has a thirty-year mortgage."

"He does."

"And he *owes* this money. To a bank. For thirty years."

"Yes."

Vazrath lowered the rulebook. Smoke curled from his nostrils. "Thirty years is a *nap*," he said. "I once lost a century because I closed my eyes during a thunderstorm. Why is Dennis so stressed?"

There was a pause around the table.

"Humans only live about eighty years," Morvane said gently. "So a thirty-year mortgage is more than a third of Dennis's life."

Vazrath stared at him. His tail, which had been flicking, went still.

"*Eighty?*"

"Give or take."

"And they spend thirty of them paying for a *room*?"

"A room with a kitchen," said Pip helpfully. "And some of them have a *second* room, for the toilet."

The dragon looked down at his character sheet, where a small, balding man named Dennis stood in a drawing, holding a lawn mower, looking tired. A single claw reached out and touched the picture, almost tenderly.

"Oh, Dennis," he whispered.

---

The session ran long. Pip, whose character Tyler had a podcast with four listeners, rolled a critical success on Going Viral and then wept openly when Morvane told him the number of listeners rose to *forty*. Grukk, redeemed after the parking disaster, defeated Linda from Compliance in a feat of pure negotiation, by saying "Per my last email" in a voice so deep that Morvane ruled it a Intimidation check and Linda signed off on the quarterly report without another word.

Then Morvane drew a card from the Encounter deck, and his voice dropped.

"The final challenge of the day," he said. "It is four fifty-eight on a Friday. You each need to print one document."

"That's all?" said Grukk.

"That's all."

"And what's the enemy?"

Morvane turned the card around. The art showed a squat gray machine with a single blinking light. Beneath it, in red, was a single word: **PAPER JAM.**

Nobody spoke.

"It says its DC is *twenty-five*," whispered Seraphelle.

"It doesn't tell you what's wrong with it," Morvane said. "Only that something is. The light is blinking. It will not say why."

Pip put his head in his hands. "I've faced a *beholder*," he said. "I wasn't scared of the beholder."

"Beholders," Vazrath said grimly, "have *weaknesses*."

They rolled. Pip got a six. Seraphelle got an eleven. Grukk got a four, and without being asked, quietly picked up his character sheet and whispered, "Brad is going to hit it."

"Brad *hits* it," Morvane confirmed, scribbling. "It does nothing. The light blinks."

At last Vazrath stepped forward, tiny and golden-eyed, and placed one claw on the die. For a long moment he held it, the way he had once held a kingdom's worth of treasure.

"Dennis," he said, "opens the back panel."

"Dennis doesn't know where the back panel is," said Morvane.

"Dennis has been paying a thirty-year mortgage," said the dragon. "Dennis has learned that sometimes you simply open every door until something works."

He rolled. The die bounced twice and settled.

Twenty.

The table erupted. Grukk pounded the barrel. Pip fell off his chair. Seraphelle clapped with both hands over her mouth. Morvane, who was supposed to be impartial, was seen to wipe something from the hollow of his eye.

"Dennis," the lich announced, "finds a single crumpled page wedged behind the toner. He pulls it free. The machine whirs. The light turns green. Your documents print, warm, in perfect order."

"Do we win?" said Pip.

"There's no winning," said Morvane. "You simply get to go home for the weekend."

Nobody said anything for a moment. It was the best ending any of them had ever heard.

---

Later, when the candles had burned low and the others were gathering their dice and packing up, Seraphelle found Vazrath still sitting at the table, studying the little drawing of Dennis.

"You're quiet," she said.

"I have lived four thousand years," the dragon said. "I have burned cities. I have hoarded mountains of gold. And I have never once been brave enough to do what Dennis does."

"Which is?"

"Get up on Monday." He looked up at her, and his eyes were old and wet and very bright. "Knowing it's one of only eighty years. Knowing the toaster will break, and the bank will call, and the machine will jam. And going anyway. Putting on the little shoes. Saying something about the weather."

Seraphelle sat down beside him. After a while she said, "Same time next week?"

Vazrath smiled, which on a dragon the size of a cat is a small and terrible and wonderful thing.

"Next week," he said, "I want to play someone who has a *dog*."

content:
# The Witness for the Defense

Martin Svoboda had practiced law for thirty-one years and had never once been surprised by a hearsay exception. So when he stood up in Courtroom 4B to argue against admitting the statement of Walter Pruitt, he felt, if anything, bored.

"Your Honor, the plaintiff wants the jury to hear what Mr. Pruitt told Officer Danvers at the scene. He supposedly saw my client's delivery van run a red light. But Mr. Pruitt passed away in March. I can't cross-examine him. I can't ask whether he'd had his glasses on, or how far away he stood, or whether he was even looking at the intersection." He warmed up. He had been saving this part. "The plaintiff's entire case rests on the word of a man who cannot be questioned by anyone, ever. It's absurd. It's like asking this court to take testimony from a *gravestone*."

Judge Imogen Reyes did not look up from her notes. "Your objection is noted, Mr. Svoboda. It is also the fourth time you've made it."

"Then let me make it a fifth way." He picked up a document from the table with a flourish. "In an abundance of caution, I subpoenaed Mr. Pruitt. Properly issued, properly served. If the plaintiff insists he's such a vital witness, let him come and be cross-examined like anyone else."

There was a pause. A juror in the back row snorted.

Judge Reyes finally looked up. "You subpoenaed a dead man."

"I did, Your Honor."

"How was he served?"

"I had a process server tape it to his headstone at Greenlawn Cemetery. Section F." Svoboda allowed himself a small smile. "I'd like the record to reflect that Mr. Pruitt has failed to appear, and that the court therefore cannot—"

The courtroom doors opened.

Svoboda did not turn around at first, because he assumed it was a late juror, or someone from the clerk's office. But the court reporter's hands had stopped moving, and Judge Reyes had taken off her glasses.

An elderly man walked down the center aisle. He wore a brown suit that was a little too good for the occasion and looked as though it had been pressed by someone who loved him. He was holding a folded piece of paper, weathered and damp at the corners, with a strip of packing tape still stuck to one edge. He was not translucent. He did not glow or drift. He walked with a slight limp, the way a man walks when his left hip has been bothering him for years. The only odd thing was that the air around him was a few degrees colder, and the front row smelled faintly of turned earth and carnations.

"Sorry I'm late," he said. "Parking."

Nobody spoke.

"Mr. Pruitt?" Judge Reyes said at last.

"Yes, ma'am. Walter Pruitt. I got a subpoena." He held up the paper. "Took me a while to work out what it was. The rain had gotten at it."

Svoboda found his voice somewhere near his shoes. "Your Honor, I... object. This witness is deceased."

"Yes, I noticed," said Judge Reyes. "On what grounds do you object to a witness you subpoenaed?"

"On the grounds that he's, that is, it's, he *can't*—"

"He appears to be doing it fine." She turned to the bailiff, who had gone the color of printer paper. "Deputy Alvarez, please swear in the witness."

The bailiff approached with the Bible held out at arm's length, like someone feeding a large dog. Walter put his left hand on it. His hand did not pass through. The bailiff let out a small breath.

"Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth?"

"Well," said Walter, "I don't see what I'd gain by lying at this point. But yes."

---

Dana Okafor, the plaintiff, sat at her table with her mouth open. She had spent two years in a neck brace and eleven months in physical therapy. She had been told, repeatedly and by several lawyers, that her case was very difficult.

Her attorney, a young woman named Priya Venkataraman, recovered first. "Your Honor, I'd like to note that I have no objection to Mr. Pruitt testifying."

"I imagine not," Judge Reyes said. "Mr. Svoboda, it's your subpoena. You may proceed."

Svoboda had no notes. He had prepared an entire cross-examination of a man who would not be there, and it had consisted mostly of the pause where the witness would fail to answer. He gripped the podium.

"Mr. Pruitt. You, uh. You were at the corner of Alder and Third on the afternoon of October ninth."

"At the bus stop. The 14 was running behind. It always is."

"And you claim you saw my client's van run a red light."

"I don't claim it. I saw it." Walter's voice was mild. "Light turned red, oh, a good four seconds before the van came through. I counted, because I'd just checked my watch and I was annoyed about the bus. Then there was a terrible noise, and the van hit that poor young lady's Corolla."

"You're eighty-one years old."

"I was eighty-one. Eighty-two in June, if things had gone otherwise."

A juror laughed and tried to turn it into a cough.

Svoboda pressed on. "Your eyesight, Mr. Pruitt. Isn't it true you wore bifocals?"

"I did. I had them on. I'm not wearing them now." Walter looked pleasantly around the courtroom. "Funny thing. I can see fine."

"I... no further questions."

"Mr. Svoboda," Judge Reyes said, "you have *barely* begun."

"I have no further questions, Your Honor."

---

Priya Venkataraman stood slowly, like someone approaching a very strange animal. "Mr. Pruitt, I just have a few questions. Why did you tell Officer Danvers what you saw?"

"Seemed like the thing to do. The young lady was in a bad way, and the van driver was telling everyone she'd come out of nowhere. I'd been sitting right there. It didn't seem right to let that stand." He glanced at Dana. "I stayed with you until the ambulance came, remember? I held your purse."

Dana put a hand over her mouth. "You said your name was Walt," she whispered. "You told me the bus was always late."

"It is."

"Mr. Pruitt," Priya said, "is there anything about your testimony today that differs from what you told the officer?"

"No, ma'am. Though I'll say he wrote 'approximately four seconds,' and I said *at least* four. I'd like that corrected."

"So noted," said the court reporter faintly. It was the first thing she had said all day.

---

When both sides had finished, Judge Reyes folded her hands. "Mr. Pruitt, is there anything else you'd like to tell the court?"

Walter considered this. "Only that I wasn't sure I'd be allowed. I've been sort of, well, around, since March. Mostly I sit at that bus stop. Nobody's fixed the bench, you know. It's got a bad slat. I've been meaning to call the city." He turned to Svoboda, not unkindly. "Then I got your paper, young man, and I thought, well, somebody wants to hear what I have to say. That doesn't happen as often as you'd think, at my age. Or after."

Svoboda, to his own surprise, found that he was looking at the floor.

"There's a witness fee, I believe," Walter added. "Forty dollars and mileage."

"Yes," Judge Reyes said. "Mr. Svoboda?"

Svoboda took out his wallet. He counted out two twenties and then, after a moment, a five. "For the parking," he muttered.

"Much obliged." Walter folded the bills carefully into his breast pocket. "I'll put it toward the bench."

"You may step down, Mr. Pruitt," said Judge Reyes. "The court thanks you for your service."

Walter nodded to the jury, then to Dana, then to the judge. He walked up the aisle with his slight limp and pushed through the double doors. Deputy Alvarez, after a long moment, went to look into the hallway. He came back and shook his head.

"Nothing, Judge. Just a little cold by the elevator."

"Mm." Judge Reyes put her glasses back on. "Mr. Svoboda, I'm going to rule that the officer's report is admissible as a prior consistent statement of a witness who has now, ah, testified. Do you wish to be heard?"

Svoboda looked at his client, who was staring at the ceiling. He looked at the empty aisle. He thought about thirty-one years of never being surprised.

"No, Your Honor," he said. "The defense would like to discuss settlement."

---

The jury was dismissed with the court's thanks. Afterward, the court reporter checked her transcript and found that every word of Walter's testimony had been recorded, clean and clear and time-stamped,

content:
# Zero

Walter Pruitt woke at 6:40, ten minutes before his alarm, as he had every day for twenty-two years, and lay still while the ceiling came into focus.

In the bathroom mirror, floating above his reflection's thinning gray hair, was the same number it had always been. A plain, round, unambiguous **0**.

He'd read once that the numbers appeared on everyone around age twelve, in the form of a faint shimmer that firmed up into digits. They were the color of whatever light you stood in, never bright, never dim, just *there*, like a name tag. Nobody knew why. Scientists had stopped asking and started publishing papers on what it did to marriages.

"Morning, Zero," he told the mirror, because if he didn't make the joke first, someone else would.

---

The 7:55 bus was crowded, and Walter had long ago learned the choreography. You didn't look up too quickly. You let your eyes drift across the numbers like scanning a menu. There was a teenager with **2** who kept touching the screen of his phone as though it might produce a third. A woman in scrubs carried a **41** and a thermos and the expression of someone who had earned both. A man in a very good suit wore **117**, and sat with his legs spread across a seat and a half.

And then the glance, which Walter also knew. A woman about his age got on at Fifth, scanned the aisle for a seat, and her eyes touched the top of his head. They flicked up, paused, and slid away. It lasted less than a second. It was the look people gave a house with a very old car in the driveway: not unkind, just *huh*.

Walter had catalogued the glances over the decades. There was pity, which was the worst. There was curiosity, which was tiring. There was the suspicious glance, the one that wondered what was wrong with him, or whether something was. And there was the occasional flash of something like envy, which he never understood, and which came mostly from people with very large numbers.

He looked out the window. A pigeon was eating a french fry with great dignity.

---

Walter worked in the county records office, in a basement that smelled of toner and old paper. He had done this job for twenty-six years. He knew where every deed in the county was buried, and he was good at it in the way that people are good at things when they have nothing else vying for the attention.

"Walter!" Janice from Permits leaned over the counter at 9:15, balancing a coffee. Her number, **212**, had always struck him as faintly architectural, like a building she'd been constructing for decades and was proud of. "Did you see Dennis got his number changed?"

"I did not."

"Forty-four. Up from forty-three. *Forty-four.* At the Holiday Inn Express, if you can believe it." She said this with relish. Everyone in the office tracked everyone else's number the way people in other offices tracked the weather. A jump was news. A stall was gossip. A leap of several digits in a week was grounds for a card and a cake.

"Good for Dennis," said Walter, and meant it, mostly.

"You're such a good egg." Janice patted the counter, and her eyes didn't go to his head, which he appreciated. She had stopped looking years ago, somewhere around her third divorce, and he was grateful for that small mercy more than he'd ever told her.

The new intern, Priya, came by with a stack of files at eleven. She was twenty-two and carried a **3** that she wore like a borrowed coat, uncertain of the fit. She was the type to try very hard at not looking, which meant she looked in short, panicky bursts.

"Mr. Pruitt, can I ask you something?"

"You may."

"Is it—" She stopped and started over. "Do people ever say stuff to you? About it?"

Walter set down his stamp. He could have deflected. Instead, because she was young and her face was honest, he said, "Mostly they don't say anything. That's the thing. The saying would almost be easier."

Priya nodded slowly. "My grandmother says it's nobody's business. That the number's just a *fact*, not a *grade*."

"Your grandmother sounds like a wise woman."

"She's got a **9**," Priya said, as if it settled something. "She says it was the right nine."

Walter laughed, a real one, and Priya relaxed, and for a moment the basement felt less like a basement.

---

He ate lunch in the small park across from the courthouse, on the third bench from the fountain, which had been his bench for as long as he'd worked there. A little girl with a shimmering, baby-soft **0** was feeding crusts to ducks, and her father, a tired man with **6**, nodded at Walter the way strangers nod when they're both pretending the world is simpler than it is.

Zeros were everywhere in the park, and they were all children. Walter had thought about that often. A zero was ordinary until about sixteen, then charming until twenty, then a little embarrassing until thirty, and after that it became a kind of weather, something people stopped bringing up. By fifty, it was a monument.

He had not, as far as he could tell, ever *decided* any of it. That was what no one understood. There had been no vow, no tragedy. There had been a mother who got sick when he was twenty-six and stayed sick for nineteen years, and a man who rearranged his whole life around her care the way water rearranges itself around a stone. There had been a girl named Constance in his thirties, and a long dinner, and a hand on his arm, and a moment where he'd said, *I should get home, Mother's alone*, and had known as he said it that he was choosing the easy door.

After his mother died, he was forty-five. He looked up one day and everyone had gone ahead without him, like a train that left the station while he was checking the timetable.

It wasn't that he didn't want it. He did, sometimes, in an abstract and aching way, like wanting to see a country he'd never visited. But wanting was a muscle, and he had not used it, and it had gone quiet.

---

The afternoon was files, and a man who needed a copy of a 1974 easement and who stared at Walter's head for the entire transaction with the frank wonder of someone at a zoo.

"Can I help you with something else, sir?" Walter asked mildly.

"No," said the man. "No, I just—" He gestured vaguely, then at his own **58**, as if it might explain him. "Never mind."

"Have a good day," said Walter. He had said it ten thousand times, and he put into it, as always, exactly as much kindness as the man deserved, plus a little more.

---

On the way home, the bus was emptier. Walter got off a stop early, which he did on Thursdays, and walked to the little community garden behind the Methodist church, where he rented a plot the size of a door. He grew tomatoes. They were not good tomatoes. He loved them anyway.

There was someone at the plot next to his, kneeling in the dirt with a trowel and a sun hat. A woman, late forties or early fifties, gray braid, sleeves pushed up. She was struggling with a stubborn weed, and she glanced up when his shadow fell across her.

Her number, hovering faintly above the brim of the hat, was **0**.

Neither of them said anything for a moment. It was the strangest feeling, being *seen* in a way he hadn't been since he was a boy. She wasn't doing the glance. She wasn't doing anything. She was just looking at him, the way you look at someone who's come into a room you thought only you knew about.

"I'm Ruth," she said.

"Walter."

"I just got this plot. I don't know a thing about tomatoes."

"Neither do I," said Walter. "Twenty years, and I still don't. But they come up anyway. That's the secret, I think. They just come up."

Ruth laughed, short and surprised. She sat back on her heels and wiped her forehead with the back of her wrist, leaving a smudge of dirt. "Do you want to see what I did wrong?"

"Absolutely," said Walter, and crossed the invisible border between their plots.

---

He did not go home with her. Nothing so tidy or so cinematic happened. They talked about soil and the unreasonable price of stakes and whether the church would ever fix the spigot. At one point she said, almost to the dirt, "I used to hate it. The number. I used to think it was a sentence being read aloud about me."

"And now?"

She considered. "Now I think it's just a number. It's not the *story*. The story's longer."

Walter looked at the tomato plants, small and crooked and stubbornly green, and at the woman beside him, and at the light going gold over the church roof.

"Same time next Thursday?" he said.

"I'll bring better stakes."

He walked home with dirt under his fingernails. On the bus, a teenager glanced at the top of his head, then away. Walter found, to his mild surprise, that he didn't mind. He watched the city slide by in the window, and in the dark glass he caught his own reflection, the gray hair, the tired eyes, and above it all the faithful little **0**, unchanged.

It looked, for the first time in a long while, less like an ending than like a number at the start of a count.

content:
# A440

The first thing Ines notices is that the radiator is out of tune.

It has always been out of tune, of course. For eleven winters it has ticked and sighed in the corner of the bedroom, somewhere between a B-flat and a B, a sour in-between note that would have driven her mad if she hadn't loved it. Tonight it sounds almost tender.

*Funny,* she thinks. *The things that come to you.*

She had expected something grander. For years she'd pictured it, the way you do when you're old and the future has narrowed to a single door: a great review of her life, faces rising out of the dark like lanterns. Instead her mind is a cluttered kitchen drawer, and it keeps handing her small, odd objects.

The tomatoes. Someone needs to stake the tomatoes. She put in six plants in May, and by now they'll be sprawling and heavy and falling over themselves. She tries to say this aloud, but the words stay where they are. In the chair by the window, her granddaughter Pilar looks up from her phone anyway, as if she'd heard.

"Abuela?"

Ines wants to say *it's nothing, go back to your phone, I like the little blue light on your face.* What comes out is a breath. Pilar takes her hand and holds it carefully, as though it were a bird.

*Such good hands,* Ines thinks, *and she doesn't know it yet.* They are long-fingered and square at the tips. Pilar could have played anything, but she chose to study law, and that is fine, that is fine. Ines made her peace with it years ago. Almost.

---

Sixty-one years she tuned pianos. People are surprised when she tells them what the work really is. They imagine it is about making a piano *right*, but there is no right. A piano is a compromise, a negotiation among notes that don't quite agree. Tune the fifths pure and the thirds go sour. Tune the thirds sweet and the fifths grow restless. What you do is spread the disagreement around, a little here and a little there, so that no one can hear any single place where it hurts. A good tuning is a well-distributed lie, and the lie lets you play in every key.

She thinks that might be the whole secret of a marriage, too. She thinks that might be the secret of Tomás, who snored, who never learned to fold a fitted sheet, who sang flat in the shower every morning for forty years, and whom she loved with the entire unreasonable width of her chest. They had not been in tune. They had spread it around.

Tomás has been dead six years, and she realizes now, with great clarity, that she has been listening for him all that time. She has heard him in the garage, in the hinge of the screen door, in the particular hush of the house after dinner. She never told anyone. It seemed greedy to ask the world to give back what it had already taken.

*Soon,* she thinks, and the word has no fear in it at all, which surprises her. She checks for fear the way you pat a pocket for keys. Nothing. Only a vast, mild curiosity, like standing at the edge of a lake in the early morning.

---

The radiator ticks. Somewhere below, a door closes. Her son's voice murmurs in the hall, low and cracked. He is trying not to cry where she can hear him, and she loves him for it and wishes he wouldn't bother.

There are things she should be thinking about, she supposes. Regrets. People always say you'll have regrets. She turns them over dutifully. The sister she didn't call back. The year she was so tired that she was short with the children. A concert in Vienna she never went to because the tickets were dear and the timing was wrong, and then the timing was always wrong.

But the regrets are light. They don't weigh what they used to. They are like the leaves she used to find inside old uprights: a pencil, a button, a child's lost coin, small things that fell in through the years and sat there in the dark, harmless, part of the instrument now.

What weighs something, what has *mass*, is the other category. The first time she heard a piano brought to true pitch, when she was nineteen and apprenticed to a bad-tempered Hungarian named Mr. Varga, and the whole room seemed to *settle*, like a sigh from the walls. The smell of Tomás's jacket. Pilar at four years old, standing on the bench and hitting a single key over and over, announcing, "This one is *my* one." The sound of rain on the roof of the first apartment. Her mother's hands in dough.

*That's it,* she thinks. *That's the whole list. It's enough. It was always enough, I just didn't count it.*

---

Her breathing has changed. She can tell because the room has grown very spacious, and the sounds in it have grown pure, like tones with the overtones stripped away. The radiator. The clock. Pilar's quiet breathing, which she matches for a moment, then loses.

Mr. Varga used to carry a tuning fork in his vest pocket, an old steel one, and he would strike it against his knee and hold it to the bone behind his ear, so the sound seemed to come from inside his own skull. *A,* he would say. *Four-forty. Everything else you can argue about. This, you don't argue.*

She hears it now. Faint, then clear, a single clean note with nothing to compare itself to. It isn't coming from the room. It is coming, she understands, from the inside, from behind the ear, from the bone.

She had wondered what she would feel at the end, and the answer is very simple. She feels *in tune.* Not perfectly. Nothing is perfect, and she would be suspicious if it were. But the disagreements have been spread around so evenly, so patiently, over so many years, that she cannot find the place where it hurts.

"I'm here," Pilar is whispering. "I'm here, Abuela, I'm here."

*I know,* Ines thinks. *I can hear you. You're my one.*

The note holds, steady and bright, and she follows it out as far as it will go.

content:
**The Talk (Reversed)**

I had rehearsed it in the bathroom mirror eleven times. The best version went: *Mom, Dad, I have some news, and I need you to hear the whole thing before reacting.*

The problem was that nobody in the history of my family had ever heard the whole thing before reacting.

"Dinner's ready!" Mom called up the stairs.

I looked at the three positive tests hidden in my sock drawer, then at the pamphlet the clinic had given me. It was titled *Male Gestational Carriers: What to Expect*, and it had a stock photo of a smiling guy in a flannel shirt cradling his belly. He looked way too happy. He was clearly not seventeen and clearly not about to tell his father.

"Coming!" My voice cracked on the second syllable. Great start.

---

Dinner was meatloaf, which is a good-news food in our house. Bad news gets takeout, because Mom doesn't cook angry. I took it as a small mercy.

Dad was telling a story about a guy at work who'd microwaved fish in the break room. Mom was nodding. My little sister Josie was feeding green beans to the dog under the table, and nobody was stopping her.

I put my fork down. "So. I need to tell you something."

Mom's eyes went right to me. Mothers have radar for that tone. "Okay."

"And I need you to let me finish."

Dad set down his water. "Are you in trouble?"

"Sort of. Not like police trouble." I took a breath. "Maya and I have been together for almost a year, which you know."

"We like Maya," Dad said carefully, in the voice of a man bracing for that to change.

"You know how the doctor said my, um..." I waved a hand at my midsection. "My situation. The thing from when I was twelve."

The room went still. When I was twelve, a routine physical turned into a lot of specialist appointments and one very long word, *gestational-capable*. It's rare, about one in forty thousand guys. I'd been told it was basically a trivia fact about my body, like being double-jointed.

"The doctor said it was extremely unlikely," Mom said slowly.

"Yeah. Extremely unlikely is not the same as impossible."

Nobody moved. Josie stopped feeding the dog.

"I'm pregnant," I said. "Maya's the... I mean, we're both... It's ours. I'm about nine weeks. I took three tests, then went to the clinic Tuesday, and they confirmed it."

Silence. The fridge hummed. The dog, sensing an opportunity, ate a green bean off the floor.

Dad opened his mouth, closed it, and opened it again. "Nine weeks," he said, like a man reading a foreign road sign.

"Yes."

"As in *weeks*."

"Yes."

"Of a *baby*."

"That's usually what it is, Dad."

He nodded. Then he stood up, walked to the kitchen counter, picked up the salt shaker, looked at it for a long moment, and set it back down. "I'm going to need a minute," he said, and walked out the back door.

Through the window I watched him stand in the yard with his hands on his head, looking at the sky like it owed him an explanation.

---

Mom hadn't moved. I braced myself, because her silences were worse than Dad's walking outside.

"Look at me," she said.

I did. I was already crying a little, which was embarrassing.

"Are you okay? Physically? Are you sick, are you in pain?"

That wasn't what I expected. "I'm... kind of nauseous in the mornings. And I cried at a dog food commercial yesterday."

"You cry at all the commercials."

"Okay, true."

She almost smiled, and then didn't. "Does Maya know?"

"She was with me at the clinic. Her parents don't know yet. She's telling them tonight, too. She said if I told you first, she'd feel less like we were—" I wiped my face on my sleeve. "I'm so sorry. I know this isn't what you wanted for me. You've got plans for me, college and everything, and I know I messed it all up."

"Hey." Mom reached across the table and took my hand, which she hadn't done since I was about ten. "Stop. Listen to me. I'm not going to pretend I'm not scared, because I am. I'm terrified. But you didn't mess up my love for you. That's not a thing you can do."

That was when I really started crying, the ugly kind with hiccups. Josie, who is eleven and has no filter, said, "Does this mean I'm going to be an aunt?"

"Yes," Mom said.

"Cool. Can I name it?"

"No," Mom and I said together.

---

Dad came back in twenty minutes later. His eyes were red, but he'd clearly given himself a talking-to out there. He sat down heavily across from me.

"I have questions," he said.

"Okay."

"Are you going to keep it? You don't have to answer that now. It's your decision, yours and Maya's. I just want you to know we're here whichever way it goes."

I nodded. "We're still figuring it out. We've talked a lot. We're leaning toward keeping it, but we're scared. And we know it's going to be hard."

"It is going to be hard," Dad said. "Very hard. I'm not going to lie to you about that."

"I know."

"You're going to need to finish school."

"I know."

"And we'll need to find a good doctor, one who's actually seen this before and isn't going to treat you like a science fair project."

"The clinic gave us a name."

"And I'm going to need to read everything ever written on this." He rubbed his face. "I just— you're my kid. You're seventeen. Yesterday you were learning to ride a bike."

"That was a long time ago, Dad."

"It was *yesterday*," he said, with total conviction, and his voice broke. Then I was up and around the table, and he was hugging me so hard my ribs creaked. Mom joined in, and then Josie, and somewhere in the pile the dog got involved.

"Careful," Mom said, laughing and crying at once. "He's carrying precious cargo."

"Mom, it's the size of a lime. I read it on the app."

"Then it's a precious lime," Dad said into my shoulder, and that set all of us off again.

---

Later, in my room, my phone buzzed. It was Maya.

*how'd it go*

I thought about it. *Dad went outside to yell at the sky. Mom held my hand. Josie wants naming rights.*

*so... good??*

*Yeah,* I typed. *I think good. You?*

A pause, then three dots, then: *my mom fainted. my dad is googling. but they're both hugging me now. so also good??*

*Good,* I wrote.

I put the phone down and rested my hand on my stomach, where nothing showed yet and everything had changed. I was still terrified, and I had no idea how any of it would work.

But downstairs I could hear my parents talking quietly in the kitchen, the scrape of chairs, the clink of Dad making tea he wouldn't drink. For the first time in nine weeks, I felt like I wasn't carrying it alone.

content:
# The Undefeated Man

Professor Paradox had been defeated four hundred and twelve times, and he had arranged for every one of them to be impossible.

Agent Mara Quill learned this in the Chronology Annex, a room that officially did not exist, from a analyst who hadn't slept since the previous Tuesday, which for him might have been next Thursday.

"It's elegant," the analyst said miserably, pointing at a whiteboard covered in looping arrows. "He didn't make himself invincible. Invincibility is crude. He made himself *load-bearing*. Every way we could beat him depends on something he did. Stop his machine, and we only know where it is because of the warning he sent. Arrest him, and the arresting officer exists only because the Professor's first crime put her parents in the same elevator. Take any thread out and the whole tapestry unravels, including the thread you pulled with."

"So if we defeat him..."

"Then we never could have. And the universe has to reconcile that. Best estimate? It doesn't reconcile. It tears." He drew a small, sad explosion on the whiteboard. "He's turned his own defeat into a doomsday device, and he's the only one with the key."

Mara looked at the arrows for a long time. "He wants us to know this."

"He sent it as a fruit basket."

---

The Professor received her in his Orrery, a cathedral-sized chamber where tiny suns orbited slowly through the air and every clock on the walls showed a different hour. He sat in a leather chair that was, by her instruments, simultaneously brand new and eight hundred years old. He was thinner than his photographs, with a gray goatee and the kind of immaculate cardigan that suggested a man who had once been very good at tenure.

"Agent Quill. Do sit. Or don't. You've already sat, in a sense, in about nine of my timelines."

"I'm not here to fight you."

"How refreshing. Everyone else tries, and the universe politely shoves them away like a bouncer with a conscience." He smiled. "You've seen the diagram. Isn't it lovely? I worked on it for forty subjective years. Do you know what I realized around year thirty?"

"That you'd run out of people to talk to?"

His smile flickered, a quarter-second of something real, and then it was back. "That *winning* is a trap. A winner can be dethroned. But a man who cannot be defeated is simply a fact, like a mountain, and nobody beats a mountain. They walk around it."

"And if I took a gun out right now?"

"You would find it was never loaded. Or that you never came. Or that you'd come and fired, and I'd been standing slightly to the left for reasons that would take the universe an unbearable amount of retroactive effort to arrange. It would *manage*. Reality is a terrible coward about paradox."

Mara did not take out a gun. She walked a slow circle around a small blue sun and said, "Tell me about the load-bearing part. Everything that could beat you depends on something you did."

"Everything."

"Everything that's an *event*."

He paused. It was a small pause, but she had spent eleven years learning to hear the pauses in other people's sentences. It was how she knew when a witness was lying and, more often, when they were frightened.

"Go on," he said.

"You built your trap out of causes. A defeat has to *happen*. Something knocks you down, and something before that made the knock possible, and so on back through time, and you've threaded your hand through every link." She stopped circling. "But a surrender isn't an event the way a defeat is. It has no cause outside of you. Nothing pushes you into it. You just... decide."

"A surrender is a defeat with better manners."

"Is it?" Mara took a folding chair from the air, because the Orrery supplied things if you stopped insisting on them, and sat down across from him. "Walk me through it. If you lay down your arms tomorrow, what's the paradox? Who's the cause? Which thread comes loose? I'm not the one who beat you. Nobody is. You simply stopped."

He opened his mouth and closed it. Around them, the little suns went on turning.

"The universe doesn't care," Mara said, "if a man changes his mind. It's the one thing it has never been able to rewind. You can't *un-decide* something for someone and have it still be theirs."

"You're proposing I give up."

"I'm proposing nothing. You're the one with the mountain. I'm just wondering why you built it so tall."

---

He did not answer for what the clocks insisted was nine minutes, three hours, and a Wednesday.

Then, quietly: "Do you know what the first thing was that I ever fixed? When I got the machine working?"

"No."

"A conversation." He turned his hand over and looked at the palm. "My wife. We had an argument the night before she died, a stupid one, about a dinner party. I went back to make it right. And I did. I made it right, and then she was in a car on the same road the next morning anyway, because the road didn't care about my apology. So I went back again. And again." He laughed, a dry little sound. "I have been to that evening six thousand times. I got very good at the conversation. I got very good at everything else too. It turns out that's what happens if you refuse to lose something: you end up stronger than anything that could take it from you, and it's still gone."

Mara said nothing. She had learned that too, in eleven years: that the best thing to say was often nothing.

"The trap was never for you," he said. "It was so that no one could ever make me *stop*. If someone defeated me, then I'd have to accept it. The universe would tell me *this is done, Alistair, it's over.* I could not bear to be told." He looked up. "So I made it so no one could tell me."

"But no one else could tell you," Mara said gently. "That's what you built. Only you could."

The Professor was quiet.

Then he stood, slowly, a thin man in a good cardigan, and walked to the wall where a single clock showed a single hour, the one that was always the same: *9:42 p.m.*, the night before. He put a hand flat on the glass.

"Yes."

"The road is still there."

"Yes."

prompt: You wait tables in a Southern bar with a cartoonishly sassy , gay , black cook and are best friends with his sister . A vampire walks in to have a drink of the new fake blood your bar sells . You can also hear people 's thoughts and you 're half human , half fairy . Who killed your grandmother ?
content:
# Synthetic

The night the vampire walked into Boudreaux's, I was carrying four baskets of fried pickles and listening to nine different people think about sex, money, and the Saints, in roughly that order.

That's the trouble with me. Most folks get to hear only what comes out of people's mouths, which is a mercy. I get the director's cut.

"Order up, baby girl!" Dorian bellowed through the kitchen pass, brandishing a spatula like a scepter. He wore a hairnet he'd bedazzled himself and a T-shirt that said **YES, I'M THE BEST THING ON THE MENU.** "And tell that man at table six that if he sends back my étouffée one more time, I will season the next batch with my *disappointment.*"

"He didn't send it back, Dorian. He thought it was too good. He's feeling guilty about his diet."

"Well." Dorian sniffed. "Good. Guilt is the secret ingredient."

His sister Renee leaned on the bar, polishing a glass that had been clean for ten minutes. She'd been my best friend since second grade, when she punched Tommy Vance for saying my mama's nerves were "catching." She was the only person in Bellmare, Louisiana, I'd ever told the truth.

"Sookie face," she muttered, which was our code for *you're doing the thing.* I wasn't allowed to say her nickname for me out loud in public, because I hated it, and she knew it.

"I'm not doing the thing."

"You're doing the head tilt."

I was. Because the bell over the door had just jingled, and I'd tilted my head to listen, and there was nothing there.

Not a murmur. Not a flicker. Just a hole in the noise, shaped like a man.

He was tall and pale in the way of someone who'd been pale on purpose for a long time. He wore a gray coat that was out of fashion in about 1890 and back in again by accident. He crossed the bar like the floor had been laid for him, took the stool at the end, and said in a voice like a cello being polite:

"I understand you've begun serving the synthetic."

Behind me, the whole bar went quiet. Then it went loud, because people think louder than they talk, and what they thought was *vampire vampire vampire oh Lord he's in HERE.*

Renee set down the glass. "We have Nightcap, Type O. Four dollars. Warmed or room temperature."

"Warmed."

She microwaved it with the dignity of a woman performing a sacrament. He took the first sip, closed his eyes, and the hole in the noise rippled.

"Dreadful," he said, with great satisfaction. "Thank you."

I should have gone back to my tables. Instead I stood there staring like a fool, because I'd never in my life been so close to *quiet.* It felt like cold water on a sunburn.

His eyes opened and found me. They were the gray of old coins.

"You're staring, Miss Maddox."

"I never told you my name."

"It's on your tag." He smiled slightly. "But I would have known you anyway. You smell of Odile."

Everything in my chest went still.

My grandmother, Odile Maddox, had been found on her kitchen floor three weeks ago, with the back door open and her good silver scattered across the linoleum. Sheriff Pruitt said burglary gone wrong. Sheriff Pruitt said a lot of things.

"Don't you say her name," I said.

"Sookie." Renee had come up beside me, hand on my elbow, the way she did when I was about to swing something. "Baby."

"She was my grandmother."

"I know," said the vampire. "She was my friend."

---

We talked in the back, behind the dumpsters, where the air smelled like fryer oil and magnolia. Dorian stood in the doorway with a cast-iron skillet held casually at hip level, like an accessory.

"Let me be clear," Dorian told the vampire. "I have a great deal of love in my heart and a great deal of iron in my hand, and I'm prepared to distribute both."

"I would expect nothing less," said the vampire, whose name was Anselm. "Your cooking is the only reason I tolerate this parish."

"You've never eaten my cooking."

"I've smelled it. It was enough."

Dorian considered this. "I'll allow it."

I folded my arms. "How did you know my grandmother?"

"She was half fairy, as you are. Her mother's line." He said it plainly, as though he were mentioning a family recipe. "She came to me forty years ago, young and frightened, to ask what the hunger in men's eyes meant when they looked at her. I told her. In return, she kept me company through a very long and very dull century. We played cards on Thursdays."

I laughed, and it came out wet. Nana had gone out *every* Thursday. She'd told me it was her sewing circle.

"She was careful," Anselm said. "She never let me near enough to be tempted, and I never asked. But you must understand what she was. To my kind, fairy blood is like sunlight in a bottle. It lets us walk in daylight, for an hour, for a day. There are people who would pay *anything.*"

"The synthetic," Renee said slowly. "That's why you came tonight. It's killing the market."

"It is *ending* the market. Before Nightcap, a vial of the real thing would fetch ten thousand dollars. Now vampires can feed without hunting, and the desperate ones, the ones who want the sun, are the only buyers left." His gaze came back to me. "Someone has been supplying them. Someone local. I've been tracing it for months, and three weeks ago the trail led to Odile's kitchen. I arrived an hour too late."

The back of my neck prickled. "You were *there?*"

"I found her. Still warm." His voice stayed even, but the quiet around him changed, thickened, like a held breath. "I did not touch her, and I did not stay, because I heard the man running. I only saw his boots."

"What kind of boots?"

"Black. Silver tips on the toes."

I knew those boots.

Everyone in Bellmare knew those boots. But I'd stopped *seeing* them, the way you stop seeing a streetlight, because they belonged to a man who'd sat on a barstool two feet from me every Friday for six years.

---

Hollis Pruitt was the sheriff's younger brother and the part-owner of Boudreaux's, which was why nobody had ever asked how a man with a deputy's salary and no wife kept buying new trucks. He was a gentle-seeming person, soft around the middle, who tipped well and remembered your birthday.

He was at table six when we came back in.

I'd spent six years learning not to listen to him. His thoughts had always been so *pleasant,* all football and fishing and a kind of wistful loneliness, that I'd let them wash past me like warm bathwater. Now I opened myself up, wide, the way I'd been taught never to do in a crowd. The noise hit me like a wave. I ignored it all and reached for one voice.

*...told her it was just a little. Just a few vials. She'd never miss it. Stubborn old woman, sitting on a gold mine and baking pies.*

My knees nearly went.

*...didn't mean for her to fall. Just wanted the key to the cellar. Just wanted the cellar...*

"Dorian," I said, very quietly, without turning around. "Table six."

"Mm-hm," he said, and I heard the skillet shift in his hand.

Hollis looked up. He saw my face, then Anselm's behind me, and his own face did something small and terrible, like a shade being pulled down.

"Now, Sookie," he said. "Honey. Whatever he's told you, he's a *vampire.*"

"I know what he is." My voice shook. "And I know what you are. You went to her house for the cellar. For whatever she kept down there."

"I don't know what you—"

*The tree. The tree behind the house. She planted it with the old blood in the roots. It's where the fairy light comes from. I only needed a cutting, just a cutting—*

"The *pear tree,*" I said.

The color left his face.

I hadn't even known. All my life I'd thought Nana's pear tree was just a pear tree. It bloomed in January. It bore fruit in the dead of winter, sweet as syrup, and she gave it away in pies and never explained. I'd been eating fairy light my whole childhood and calling it dessert.

Hollis bolted.

He made it three steps toward the door before Renee, who had been a state-champion shot-putter for two years running, hit him with a full tray of frozen daiquiris. Then Dorian arrived with the skillet. I won't describe what happened next, except that it rang like a church bell, and that afterward Dorian looked down at the sprawled, sticky-sweet figure on the floor and remarked, "Honey, you should've stayed for dessert."

---

They arrested Hollis that night, and his brother the sheriff turned out to have known more than he'd let on, which gave everyone in town something new to think loudly about for months.

I sat on the back steps afterward with a basket of leftover fried pickles and a bottle of warm Nightcap that Anselm had set beside me without comment.

"I don't drink that," I said.

"It's not for you. It's so I have an excuse to sit here."

So he sat, and the quiet around him settled over me like a blanket. I realized I'd been holding my shoulders up around my ears for twenty-six years.

"She'd have liked you," he said after a while. "Your Dorian. Your Renee. She worried you had no one."

"She always said that," I whispered. "Whenever I'd come home from school having heard everything. She said *you'll find your people, cher. They'll be the ones who make you forget to listen.*"

Inside, Dorian had started singing something very loud and very off
